Messages.Author: tb...@lainet.com
Messages.Body:
I guess it's about time I put in my 2 cents about Ian Forestal.

As the game stands right now this card seems to powerful. It is not a
game breaker, but it would give the guy who gets it out (if its not
contested) an advantage. If Ian had to burn a blood each time he used
his power it would in my opinion solve the problem.

As for the design team trying to destroy the game: I don't think this is
the case at all. I agree the design team has made some major blunders
but I know they are not purposely trying to ruin the game. Ian (and
Beast for that matter) are more powerful because that is the nature of
expansions. I am impressed that despite the power of many vamps and
cards in DS and AH that jyhad has still maintained balance. The
escalation will continue, but the question is if the design team manages
to keep the game balanced despite it. So far they have in my opinion.

I think it is still to soon to judge the design team until we see all of the
Sabbat vamps and cards. Until then I have to wonder if there may be
something else the design team knows about that we don't.

Steve -don't call me Tom- Bucy

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On 23 Aug 1996 tb...@lainet.com wrote:

> As for the design team trying to destroy the game: I don't think this is
> the case at all.

Neither do I. I do think they seem to be almost doing so inadvertently,
however. As Alec Chang put it, it saddens me to think thtat I know the
game better than the Design Team.

> I agree the design team has made some major blunders
> but I know they are not purposely trying to ruin the game. Ian (and
> Beast for that matter) are more powerful because that is the nature of
> expansions.

That is the nature of expansions in Magic, but it need not be the nature
of all expansions. Planned obselesence is a bad thing in a CCG,
particularly in one whose strength is the relatively low $ needed to
enter and be competitive, like Jyhad.

> I am impressed that despite the power of many vamps and
> cards in DS and AH that jyhad has still maintained balance. The
> escalation will continue, but the question is if the design team manages
> to keep the game balanced despite it. So far they have in my opinion.

I think they have walked further and further towards the edge of a
cliff. Much farther, and they might just fall off.

Escalation is _NOT_ a desired thing in a balanced CCG. It is very easy
to make a card for Jyhad that is powerful or not so powerful and have it
not make an for an escalation or descalation. How? Appropriate Card
Cost and no Trump cards! (The third rule, appropriateness for game world
doesn't apply here)

If a Card like Return to Innocence is made, yes it is a powerful card.
But it hardly escalates the game when one considers its cost. (A well
done card.) Had it not had as many restrictions on use that it does, it
would be an escalation.

A card like Thoughts Betrayed _is_ an escalation (whether you think the
card is broken or not, that is a different topic) because it is a trump.
Had the card been made so that pre-range cards can be used by the
opponent, it would not be an escalation. Had its cost been increased by
1 to 2 (depending on what might be appropriate (debatable)) it would not
be an escalation.

Given that Jyhad was designed as a NL game, it escapes the escalation
problem of Magic The Gathering in redundant cards. Were magic to print
out a new version of Lightning Bolt, the power of all Red-direct damage
decks can increase, because suddenly 4 more can be used in each of those
decks. In Jyhad, you can already do this, regardless of them printing
more. (Apologies to non-Magic players if you don't understand)

Escalation then, can only come from cards overly powerful for their cost,
or cards that nullify other strategies by themselves (Archon
Investigation). These can be avoided by an acute design team.

Escalation is not desirable. I will stop playing Jyhad far before it
ever gets to the point of:
"Your using a [Bum's Rush/Faceless Night]? [Card X] makes that card
Totally Obselete"

While occasional cards may be lost (Chainsaw to Bang Nakhm, for example),
these should be the exception, rare, and not the rule.

> I think it is still to soon to judge the design team until we see all of the
> Sabbat vamps and cards. Until then I have to wonder if there may be
> something else the design team knows about that we don't.

I agree about not judging the Sabbat _set_ til we see it, but I disagree
about the Design(/Rules (???)) Team. I've seen enough of them to be
extremely disappointed by them.

Hopefully Sabbat will continue their recovery begun in AH.

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:



There was a large set of cards in Dark Sovereigns that were mostly
useless or highly underpowered. The most commonly used example is the
Werewolf Pack (a unique ally with 3 hand damage and 3 life, cannot be
hurt by melee weapons). Its cost is far too expensive (4 pool) for what
it does, especially given comparison to the renegade garou. For a while,
around here, people were doing an informal "design a _good_ werewolf
pack" contest. For the most part, except for the choices in redesign
_meant_ to be outrageous, we all agreed that our versions were each
better (all of them (!!!)).

There were a few cards in Dark Sovereigns that were underpriced. The
point system in the Jyhad set for vampire costs was relatively strictly
adhered to with few exceptions. Francois Villon has always been a good
example, and others crop up as well. The point costs of certain powers
(+1 stealth for all actions on Rebekka) was underpowered (I believe TOM
(Wylie) said that it was 1 pt. (!!!).

Debate continues whether certain cards (e.g., Thoughts Betrayed) were
broken, but many of the cards simply don't have a place in a Jyhad-like
card setting. Global effects (as Curt Adams, I believe, has written)
were typically rare, self-damaging or possibly with backfire, or
Malkavian (or all of the above). The usefulness of cards like sudden
reversal and arson went down with the sudden propagation of destroyable
master cards (rare in Jyhad) and locations easily destroyed (for much
pool investment).

On the whole, DS didn't really break Jyhad in any manner. It was simply
a set that was horribly designed.



The best expansions are those which add new aspects to the game
without altering the balance. The Setites' corruption powers
are an example of this, done well (kudos to the Design
Team). The Giovanni dumpster diving powers are another example.
Power levels don't have to be boosted, if interesting
things get added to the game. More interesting stuff will sell
better than more powerful stuff, too. Especially in the
long run (power boosting is good for an expansion or two
at best).

>Escalation is _NOT_ a desired thing in a balanced CCG. It is very easy
>to make a card for Jyhad that is powerful or not so powerful and have it
>not make an for an escalation or descalation. How? Appropriate Card
>Cost and no Trump cards! (The third rule, appropriateness for game world

>ever gets to the point of:
>"Your using a [Bum's Rush/Faceless Night]? [Card X] makes that card
>Totally Obselete"

I heartily agree! I quit playing Magic because it got filled with
'trump' cards and unbalanced strategies. WotC tried to fix problems
with trump cards, which are much less fun to play with or against.

I hope this doesn't happen with Jyhad, but I worry. Especially
since WotC seems to have decided to deal with weak sales by
escalation (in Magic, at least - Alliances). This is a
short-term strategy which will ultimately kill the game. I
hope they're not so stupid as to try this with V:TES, too.

--
Tom Doehne

Messages.Author: tb...@lainet.com
Messages.Body:
In article <8408294...@dejanews.com> <Pine.NXT.3.91.960823154037.1096B-100000@pentose> <4vv9g2$p...@reuter.cse.ogi.edu>,


About escalation: I wholeheartedly agree escalation on the order of
Tragic: The Gathering (trump card, trump the trump card, trump the
trump trump card, etc.) is ridiculous and I never want Jyhad to get
close to that point. However I think some escalation makes the game
more interesting.

Cards like increased strength, Ankara citadel Turkey, scorpion sting,
dog pack, and parthenon are all escalation. They increase power, give
abilities that where not possible, or eliminate some weaknesses a clan
may have had. I don't find these cards harmful to the game. They just
improve strategies and add new possibilities to the game.

Trump cards like archon investigation and thoughts betrayed are also
escalation. However they are the type of escalation that can harm the
game. These cards can ruin entire strategies.

I don't see Ian Forestal as the type of escalation that will hurt the
game. It is true he totally breaks the point system but in application he
is not the winning trump card. He will allow for unusual tricks and
strategies but his presence will not give anyone a huge advantage.
Ian's presence will not ruin the game.

It is to early to tell but Beast the Leatherface of Detroit may actually be
more escalation than Ian. Beast is a 7 blood vamp, has +1 hand
damage, a built in rush, superior potence, and celerity. His
disadvantage doesn't allow him to equip or recruit. In DCI environment
this guy could make rush decks a living hell to deal with. Unless the
Sabbat contains more S:CE and other anti combat measures Beast
himself could cause a real escalation in combat. I don't know if that
type of escalation is good.

I think the level of escalation in DS and AH has been ok with the
exception of a couple of cards. If the worst escalation in The Sabbat is
Ian Forestal IMO I don't think we have anything to worry about.



Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
There are 2 trump cards that spring to mind. First, of caurse, is our
dear friend Thoughts Betrayed at superior. "Opponent cannot play any
combat cards for the duration of the combat. "

This is way out of place in Jyhad. First, Jyhad combat without cards is
like chess without pieces - nothing like normal Jyhad. Second, obviously,
there is almost never anything you can do about it - because once it's
played, you can't play cards. Third, it's outrageously out of place. In
the original set, the closest card is Fast Reaction. There is no
comparison. While TB's cost of 2 blood is more than FR's cost of an extra
minion action, FR prevents *1* kind of combat card for *1* round, while TB
prevents *all* cards for *all* rounds.

The other trump is Archon Investigation. Again, there's nothing you can
do about an Investigation. In addition, the effect is incredibly out of
line with pre-existing Jyhad cards. The worst a master could do before
was send a vampire to torpor or waste 2 actions (Ectasy Laced Blood).
This one burns a vampire, with no recourse, for nothing more than using
one common Dominate card at superior.

The original set, BTW, did have at least one trump in it - Strike: Combat
Ends. There has always been a level of frustration with the fact the S:CE
is so cheap and so hard to prevent. The fact that TB does provide a way
around this is one of the few benefits it brings to the game. However,
S:CE isn't of the order of TB or AI as it is purely defensive, and doesn't
harm the opponent.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
[snip well-spoken anti-TB remarks]

I agree with you completely. I am now going to reiterate the
now-so-famous it has my name attached to it
James-Hamblin's-rant-against-cards-that-make-you-
unable-to-play-the-game.

As people who have read my posts often enough know, I own substantial
amounts of 3 card games: Magic, Jyhad, and Shadowfist. They know this
because I often refer to them for design/game-play
precedents/intuition. I don't really play Magic anymore. Why? Well, I
got sick of all of the type-1 munchkin-weenies killing before I could
breathe with cards I could never afford. Where 12-year olds get the
money for Moxes, I'll never know... But, anyway. The out-of-print
out-of-control way-too-powerful cards have the effect of leaving the
other player out of the loop. One player has an immense advantage due
to their having card that I do not. Even if my deck is a fun,
well-designed deck, it will get trounced. 100%. For sure. Why?
Counterspells. Discard. The other player prevents me from having any
cards at all, and the ones I do manage to make are "unmade" at a far
lower cost than I spent. So I do not get to play the game. I get to
try, but it doesn't get me anywhere.

So, why do I still play Shadowfist? Shadowfist has counterspells.
Shadowfist has discard. Because in Shadowfist, there are ways around
those strategies. Suffice to say that someone can still be a slimeball,
but it is not as aggravated as in Magic.

But this is not a newsgroup about other card games. This is about
Jyhad. And this post is about "trump" cards. Cards which, like
counterspells and discard in Magic, prevent the other player from
playing the game. One such card is Thoughts Betrayed. One player plays
it. The other player might as well go get a coke while his vampire gets
killed, since he can't do a damn thing about it. "Well, I'm glad that
you get to play this game. Let me know when you're finished preventing
me from playing." I hate this card. I despise it. I think that it
goes against any semblance of balance and fairness in the game.

I shudder to think of the following combo which can be easily pulled off
by our good friend Ian Forrestal: Thoughts Betrayed, Apparition, Claws
of the Dead. Look, I spent 4 blood, and you die. Hell, why not stick a
couple Theft of Vitae in there while we're at it. Wouldn't want good
ol' Ian having to lose any blood.

Before the publish of Ian, this combo would be unthinkable and
hallaciously difficult to pull off. You'd need superior dominate,
superior thau. if you wanted the theft of vitae, chimerstry and
protean. But Ian has all of that built right in. But we're not talking
about Ian (or are we...?)

Anyway, that's my rant about TB.

> The other trump is Archon Investigation. Again, there's nothing you can
> do about an Investigation.

[snip]

> This one burns a vampire, with no recourse, for nothing more than using
> one common Dominate card at superior.

OK, it'd be easy for me to say "but Archon Investigation is different!
If you're bleeding me for more than 3, you deserve what you get!", and,
in some sense, I do feel that way, but I have legitimate reasons for
liking AI.

Anti-S&B was a little hard to come by before V:tES. Unless you had
Dominate or Auspex, you can't bounce the bleeder; you had to deal with
it yourself. Which presents you with a number of options:

Bounce it: Nuff said. This include Tel. Counter.
Block it: unless the S&Ber is unlucky, you do not have as much intercept
as they have stealth. Yes, you will be able to get away with this
occasionally, but even so, you also have S:CE to worry about even if you
do get into combat. And besides; you have Auspex. Just bounce it.
Take it: Oh, look. You were just bled for 7. Again.
"Race": By which I mean "kill your prey before you get killed". Hmm,
seems to me like the fastest way to oust a prey is with S&B. Hmm, you
could be using Dominate, in which case you could just bounce it, or
Presence, in which case you are probably using Toreador, in which case
you could just bounce it.
Beat 'em Up: Rush their vampires. Well, then you have to deal with S:CE
and Obedience. The latter you can't even deal with at all, so don't
bother. I'll talk about that more later. S:CE can be dealt with with
Immortal Grapple (rare), Hidden Lurker (inefficient), and Dog Pack
(rare/expensive). I say that hidden lurker is inefficient since it
effects can be avoided by simple maneuvers. If you are the Nosferatu,
you have 1 (count them, 1) maneuver card given by your disciplines, and
if you are Malkavian, Bounce It.

So, S&B is hard for the following clans to deal with:

Brujah, Gangrel, Nosferatu, Assamite, FoSet (although Obf/Pre bleed
might be fast enough), Ravnos.

Sure these clans have various ways of _trying_ to deal with S&B, but
these usually require devotion of an entire deck to even have a fighting
chance. AI gives an escape hatch. It gives S&B a liability, something
to be wary of, which it never really had before. There was never any
reason _not_ to bleed for 7 instead of 3. Now there is. That's a good
thing in my book.

> The original set, BTW, did have at least one trump in it - Strike: Combat
> Ends. There has always been a level of frustration with the fact the S:CE
> is so cheap and so hard to prevent. The fact that TB does provide a way
> around this is one of the few benefits it brings to the game. However,
> S:CE isn't of the order of TB or AI as it is purely defensive, and doesn't
> harm the opponent.

Unless you call being screwed not being harmed. A Gangrel rush combat
deck in the original set was completely unviable due to S:CE. Now they
have Dog Pack which is expensive, but reasonably effective. But no.
S:CE is not by any means purely defensive; offensively it can be used to
devastating effect.

The other trump card which I am surprised has not been mentioned is
Obedience. There is absolutely nothing that you can do about this
card. Nothing. Zip. Zero. You just suck. Sit down. My vampire
doesn't tap, yours does, and your action fails. What could be more of a
trump card? Once again, your one card has cost you 1 card (didn't even
tap your stinking vampire) and tapped my vampire possilby wasting an
action card or action modifiers.

Well, rant mode off now. Thanks for reading.

James

>Sure these clans have various ways of _trying_ to deal with S&B, but
>these usually require devotion of an entire deck to even have a fighting
>chance. AI gives an escape hatch. It gives S&B a liability, something
>to be wary of, which it never really had before. There was never any
>reason _not_ to bleed for 7 instead of 3. Now there is. That's a good
>thing in my book.

I disagree -- it's an unnecessary hoser. And it's hardly the devotion
of an entire deck. Bleed bounce is useful against all bleeds, not just
S&B. A good way to deal with Bruise& Bleed decks if you're running
a non-combat deck. And the cards you use in a Rush combat deck
are the same ones you use to rush voters and blood machines. Ventrue
vote decks are no less a problem to a rush deck than a Malk S&B....

[snip >>S:CE is a trump card....]

>> around this is one of the few benefits it brings to the game. However,
>> S:CE isn't of the order of TB or AI as it is purely defensive, and doesn't
>> harm the opponent.

>Unless you call being screwed not being harmed. A Gangrel rush combat
>deck in the original set was completely unviable due to S:CE. Now they
>have Dog Pack which is expensive, but reasonably effective. But no.
>S:CE is not by any means purely defensive; offensively it can be used to
>devastating effect.

The Gangrel had problems with S:CE, although lots of Haven Uncovered
and dog-piling helped. Brujah have no trouble with it: IG, Psyche,
and Haven Uncovered all use up those S:CE, and are handy in
other contexts.

>The other trump card which I am surprised has not been mentioned is
>Obedience. There is absolutely nothing that you can do about this
>card. Nothing. Zip. Zero. You just suck. Sit down. My vampire
>doesn't tap, yours does, and your action fails. What could be more of a
>trump card? Once again, your one card has cost you 1 card (didn't even
>tap your stinking vampire) and tapped my vampire possilby wasting an
>action card or action modifiers.

I very much disagree. My favorite deck is a Brujah rush deck. It
routinely makes mincemeat of the Malk S&B decks in our group. If
they pack a lot of Obedience, they jam up with Obedience and
get killed by the intercept combat decks. If they don't, the
Rush decks get them. Obedience is only useful for stopping
Rush combat, and in Intercept run-away combat.

I deal with them by using Haven Uncovered. If they have 3-4
Obedience in hand, they deserve to survive. If they don't,
their vampire is toast. But that many Obedience in a deck
is a good way to get hand jammed.

--
Tom Doehne
doe...@cse.ogi.edu

Messages.Author: Drake Coker
Messages.Body:
[snip - many sensible comments about TB being too powerful]

I too think that Thoughts Betrayed is too good for its
cost, but perhaps not as much as everyone else. It seems
to me that TB really hoses two strategies: S:CE and combat
decks that use combat cards. Hosing S:CE is nice - S:CE is
pretty hard to stop. Hosing combat cards has the (potentially)
interesting effect of making weapon decks more viable. Weapon
decks generally don't care about TB (with some exceptions).
In my group, weapon decks had fallen out of favor because
combat-card decks were working better.

TB also has the effect of making weenie vampires more attractive.
Spending 2 on TB to disable a cost 1 or 2 vampire is often
not terribly effective.

Other deck designs don't care much about TB. S&B and Political
decks generally don't do much with combat. On the other hand,
TB does hose any S:CE those decks might have, so it is not
completely neutral.

Overall, I think TB is too powerful, and definitely counts
as a trump card since it hoses some strategies while ignoring
others.

So, how would everyone "fix" it. I think it might be
enough to make the cost 3 blood. Alternatively (and, I think
preferably), I might change the text so that it only prevents
Strike cards from being played (thus allowing manuevers, presses,
ammo cards, Diguised Weapon and Blood to Water). Any ideas/opinions?

- Drake

Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
> I too think that Thoughts Betrayed is too good for its
> cost, but perhaps not as much as everyone else. It seems
> to me that TB really hoses two strategies: S:CE and combat
> decks that use combat cards.

Don't mix words. TB hoses combat decks period. More on this later.

> Hosing S:CE is nice - S:CE is
> pretty hard to stop.

Yes it is, but I think that TB goes too far.

> Hosing combat cards has the (potentially)
> interesting effect of making weapon decks more viable. Weapon
> decks generally don't care about TB (with some exceptions).
> In my group, weapon decks had fallen out of favor because
> combat-card decks were working better.

Yes. Your group has discovered the "well-known fact" (I'm covering up
my head...) that guns don't work. They're expensive and inefficient.
Besides, who is using TB offensively? Tremere and so-called
"Euro"-Brujah. Both of which don't care about your gun. The Brujah
will Immortally Grapple you and pummel you. The Tremere will maneuver,
and play Blood Rage/Fury, so your gun doesn't work.

> TB also has the effect of making weenie vampires more attractive.
> Spending 2 on TB to disable a cost 1 or 2 vampire is often
> not terribly effective.

I don't understand this. What do you mean? If I am a combat deck using
TB offensively, I don't need to use TB to kill a little vampire with 1
or 2 points and 1 discipline? Just because I happen not to use my TB on
particular vamps doesn't make the deck less offensive.

> Other deck designs don't care much about TB. S&B and Political
> decks generally don't do much with combat. On the other hand,
> TB does hose any S:CE those decks might have, so it is not
> completely neutral.

Every deck needs to have some way to deal with combat or it will die.
Whether it be Fortitude or S:CE or what have you, they must do
something. TB neutralizes that defense. If you are in a combat and
someone plays TB, you should expect your vampire to die. Because what
can you do about it?

> Overall, I think TB is too powerful, and definitely counts
> as a trump card since it hoses some strategies while ignoring
> others.

No, no, no. It is a trump card because when you play it, you remove
your opponent from the game for a while. They can do nothing.
Nothing. Read that again. Nothing at all. You are in complete
control, and, if the deck is constructed well, when you are in complete
control, you burn the opposing vampire.

> So, how would everyone "fix" it. I think it might be
> enough to make the cost 3 blood.

3 blood, 4 blood, even 5 blood. It doesn't much matter. It is _way_
too powerful as its text is written. If it is to be fixed, the text
must be changed.

> Alternatively (and, I think
> preferably), I might change the text so that it only prevents
> Strike cards from being played (thus allowing manuevers, presses,
> ammo cards, Diguised Weapon and Blood to Water). Any ideas/opinions?

That is a possibility, and IMHO much better than simply changing the
blood cost.

Messages.Author: Dan Hollis
Messages.Body:
In article <322CF2...@cornell.edu>, je...@cornell.edu says...

>
>But this is not a newsgroup about other card games. This is about
>Jyhad. And this post is about "trump" cards. Cards which, like
>counterspells and discard in Magic, prevent the other player from
>playing the game. One such card is Thoughts Betrayed. One player plays
>it. The other player might as well go get a coke while his vampire gets
>killed, since he can't do a damn thing about it. "Well, I'm glad that
>you get to play this game. Let me know when you're finished preventing
>me from playing." I hate this card. I despise it. I think that it
>goes against any semblance of balance and fairness in the game.

First, I agree that the card is overpowered. I do, however, agree with
the direction that the card was taking, since previously, Tremere had no
effective way to deal with S:CE. Hidden Lurker, immortal grapple, all those
cards to give you a free round of combat are out of clan skills. And even
then, a hidden lurker wouldn't get you a second round strike. Tremere are
much better suited for briuse/bleed and intercept combat than rush, which does
get them into combat less than rush (your prey might take a large bleed if he
doesn't have a S:CE; and for intercept, your prey has to take blockable
actions and you must have matching intercept as well as combat). All this
made S:CE a big trump card against the Tremere.
And the NL argument against S:CE - that your opponent is going to run out,
eventually, or else he's got to have a huge % of his deck be S:CE; that
arguement can also be used for Thoughts Betrayed. How many vampires do you
expect to be trouncing, and then, with the intercept, bleed modifiers,
presses, and strikes, are you going to have the right balance of cards?
Granted, I am playing the devil's advocate a little because when you do have
the right balance, then Thoughts Betrayed is basically a ticket to torpor, or
often worse, a precursor to a Walk of Flame and a burnt vampire. The rewards
are far greater than the 'penalty' of waiting for the right 5 cards to fill
your hand.
I think maybe TB could be fairer if it didn't let your opponent strike (like
immortal grapple) but still allowed a press to end or fortitude. Or maybe
something like, your opponent cannot use cards to end combat, but could still
strike (though that eliminates the defensive use of TB).

>> The other trump is Archon Investigation. Again, there's nothing you can
>> do about an Investigation.
>[snip]

Great arguments.

>The other trump card which I am surprised has not been mentioned is
>Obedience. There is absolutely nothing that you can do about this
>card. Nothing. Zip. Zero. You just suck. Sit down. My vampire
>doesn't tap, yours does, and your action fails. What could be more of a
>trump card? Once again, your one card has cost you 1 card (didn't even
>tap your stinking vampire) and tapped my vampire possilby wasting an
>action card or action modifiers.

It also beats Thoughts Betrayed, too. And can be played by most Ventrue and
Malkavians, who fit well into decks that avoid combat.

Dan

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin <je...@cornell.edu> writes:

>I agree with you completely. I am now going to reiterate the
>now-so-famous it has my name attached to it
>James-Hamblin's-rant-against-cards-that-make-you-
>unable-to-play-the-game.

(e.g. Thoughts Betrayed and others)

One point to add to this - a card that prevents somebody from playing
makes the game not fun for them. Even if it is properly balanced (and
that is necessarily very difficult for such cards) it will be a detriment.

>So, S&B is hard for the following clans to deal with:

>Brujah, Gangrel, Nosferatu, Assamite, FoSet (although Obf/Pre bleed
>might be fast enough), Ravnos.

>Sure these clans have various ways of _trying_ to deal with S&B,

>but these usually require devotion of an entire deck to even have a
>fighting chance. AI gives an escape hatch.

Yes, it does, just as TB gives an escape hatch for S:CE. But it's the
wrong escape hatch, because it's a guillotine. Elder Intervention is a
good broadening of the anti-S&B defenses. LSJ's suggestion of AI
preventing the target from bleeding until a vote is passed is a good
hatch. AI is still out of line with the Jyhad cardset; it's still a "may
as well get a Coke" card when you're hit with it.

Incidentally, *part* of the problem with rush defenses to S&B is that S:CE
(which you complain about) is too common, cheap, and easy. The S&B decks
don't use it (apart from Settites), but enough others do to give Rush a
headache, especially if it's only part-time. This is an example of
escalating hosers - AI being devised to hadle problems partly due to an
existing hoser.

I agree with your contention that S:CE is too good, but I maintain that
it's not as bad as TB or AI.

>The other trump card which I am surprised has not been mentioned
> is Obedience.

Obedience isn't S:CE, but its effects are virtually the same (nothing
happens in combat, at superior he's tapped and you're untapped) so I have
it filed mentally with S:CE. I agree that it is also a problem, and that
many S:CE fixes will not help with Obedience.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

We already have cards that fudge with strikes. I think TB should prevent

> First, I agree that the card is overpowered. I do, however, agree with
>the direction that the card was taking, since previously, Tremere had no
>effective way to deal with S:CE. Hidden Lurker, immortal grapple, all those
>cards to give you a free round of combat are out of clan skills. And even
>then, a hidden lurker wouldn't get you a second round strike. Tremere are

What about Fast Reaction? Intercept combat, an in-clan skill. gives

in-clan card that gives them a free round of strikes.

Blood to Water/Blood Fury should do enough damage to put most vampires

second round aggro damage, but you can still use Pulled Fangs on
the first round. I'd say Tremere have less trouble with S:CE than
Gangrel. After all, some of them have Celerity (Psyche), too.

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 3 Sep 1996, James Hamblin wrote:

[Curt Adams wrote:]

> > The other trump is Archon Investigation. Again, there's nothing you can
> > do about an Investigation.
> [snip]
> > This one burns a vampire, with no recourse, for nothing more than using
> > one common Dominate card at superior.

> OK, it'd be easy for me to say "but Archon Investigation is different!
> If you're bleeding me for more than 3, you deserve what you get!", and,
> in some sense, I do feel that way, but I have legitimate reasons for
> liking AI.

This is one of those (rare) positions that we totally disagree...

> Anti-S&B was a little hard to come by before V:tES.

... and here is the statement that sets us apart. James, you bring up
several of the strategies, but to me, it seems as though either they
aren't being used in your playgroup, or you have some hideously monstrous
S&Bleeder the like of which I have never seen (and would thus love to
have on my deck archive).

>Unless you had
> Dominate or Auspex, you can't bounce the bleeder; you had to deal with
> it yourself. Which presents you with a number of options:

> Bounce it: Nuff said. This include Tel. Counter.

A very viable strategy. Tremere and Malkavians are the best at this, but
any clan with Dominate or Auspex is fine.

> Block it: unless the S&Ber is unlucky, you do not have as much intercept
> as they have stealth.

Not true. Only in environments where the only intercept is light
intercept is this true. Stealth roughly equals intercept in availability
and ease of use.

> Yes, you will be able to get away with this
> occasionally, but even so, you also have S:CE to worry about even if you
> do get into combat.

Not likely. Only the Setites have this easy combination, and their bleed
power isn't as hard to deal with as domniated bleeds. Other decks can
put this combo together (S & B & S:CE), but the work they have to invest
in it usually slows them down.

> And besides; you have Auspex. Just bounce it.
> Take it: Oh, look. You were just bled for 7. Again.

And the next time you'll likely be bled for one. This isn't a strategy
unto itself, however. Usually this is a tactic to reduce the bleeders
efficacy until you get them by other means. Note, this strategy tends to
jam the hands of high Sneak decks. Low sneak decks aren't affected, but
then they get taken out by even light intercept. The sneaker has a fine
line to walk.

> "Race": By which I mean "kill your prey before you get killed". Hmm,
> seems to me like the fastest way to oust a prey is with S&B.

Or fast vote.

> Hmm, you
> could be using Dominate, in which case you could just bounce it, or
> Presence, in which case you are probably using Toreador, in which case
> you could just bounce it.

Could is the operative word. Bouncing bleeds costs blood. Sometimes it
is better to simply race, especially with clans using Presence, who can
gain pool as they cause their prey to lose it (Via voter captivation or
presence bleeds).

> Beat 'em Up: Rush their vampires. Well, then you have to deal with S:CE
> and Obedience.

Obedience is typically more of a concern, while S:CE is something that
can be handled (and should be able to be handled) by most combat decks.
Obedience requires keeping vampires out of the action (thus, not bleeding
as fast or as much), is card and discipline intensive, and is weak
against permanent rush.

> The latter you can't even deal with at all, so don't
> bother.

See the above. Only naive combat decks "can't deal with" Obedience.

>I'll talk about that more later. S:CE can be dealt with with
> Immortal Grapple (rare), Hidden Lurker (inefficient), and Dog Pack
> (rare/expensive). I say that hidden lurker is inefficient since it
> effects can be avoided by simple maneuvers. If you are the Nosferatu,
> you have 1 (count them, 1) maneuver card given by your disciplines, and
> if you are Malkavian, Bounce It.

However, Hidden Lurker doesn't really require a manuever. The Malks
using Hidden Lurker will likely have disguised weapons, the Nossies have
sewer lids and gates, and the Assamites have their spit. Even if they do
manuever, the deck using Hidden Lurker should be toasting someone in a
non-combat deck.

You forget blood gain deck defense.

> So, S&B is hard for the following clans to deal with:

> Brujah,

Who have easy access to rush, blood gain, and occasionally (though not as
common) race.

> Gangrel,

Who have rush and intercept.

> Nosferatu,

Who have rush and intercept.

>Assamite,

Who have the most amazing rush in the game (Contracts, Haven Uncovered,
Bum's Rush, Covenant of Blood)

> FoSet (although Obf/Pre bleed might be fast enough)

It is.
They have blood gain and race.

> Ravnos.

They have rush, and the best intercept you can shake a stick at.

The above are only _typical_ strategies. My Nossie deck laughs at S&B.
Why? Because I ignore their stealth (jamming their hand), Rush their
vampires with permanent Rush (Archons), surprise rush (Bum's Rush), and
_huge_ blood gain (in mid/late game, I can gain 6 to 9 pool a turn, on
average.

> Sure these clans have various ways of _trying_ to deal with S&B, but
> these usually require devotion of an entire deck to even have a fighting
> chance.

I totally disagree with the reality of this statement. While having S&B
behind any deck in the opening is a pain, the early original loss can be
recouped. Many decks will end up directing their attention backwards
when S&B is behind them, but the same can be said of Gangrel Rush,
Ventrue Vote, or any other number of decks.

> AI gives an escape hatch.

I would call it an atomic bomb.

> It gives S&B a liability, something
> to be wary of, which it never really had before.

Looking at the above, I can think of many things it had to be wary of.

> There was never any
> reason _not_ to bleed for 7 instead of 3. Now there is. That's a good
> thing in my book.

While I agree that it is nice to have a reason not to bleed for as much,
there is such a thing as overkill. LSJ's fix is elegant (put AI on the
bleeder. That vampire cannot bleed. This card can be burned as a vote),
in that it gives reasons for S&B not to bleed, but it doesn't totally
decimate a strategy.

A long list of suggested fixes of AI has been slowly growing. It seems
to me like the only people who prefer AI as written to those suggesed are
either CL players, or they come from a CL background. My own belief is
that this is because of CLs notorious lack of a way to handle S&B, but
I'm not certain.

> then, a hidden lurker wouldn't get you a second round strike.

Both Hidden Lurker and Fast Reaction give a press at superior. As for
not giving a second round strike, you are right. The only cards that
give second round strikes are second round strike cards.

>Tremere are
> much better suited for briuse/bleed and intercept combat than rush,

> which does get them into combat less than rush (your prey might take a
> large bleed if he doesn't have a S:CE; and for intercept, your prey
> has to take blockable actions and you must have matching intercept as
> well as combat). All this made S:CE a big trump card against the Tremere.

If the Tremere are doing Rush, they need a more permanent method to deal
with S:CE. My Tremere deck uses Haven Uncovered exclusively for get into
combat. If they are intercepting, they shouldn't have a problem with S:CE.

> And the NL argument against S:CE - that your opponent is going to run out,
> eventually, or else he's got to have a huge % of his deck be S:CE; that
> arguement can also be used for Thoughts Betrayed.

Not really. The arguement only works for S:CE and Obedience because each
time a S:CE or Obedience is used, it is stopping a conflict from
happening. With each use of TB, there is a great likelihood that the
end result is the death of yet another minion.

> How many vampires do you
> expect to be trouncing, and then, with the intercept, bleed modifiers,
> presses, and strikes, are you going to have the right balance of cards?
> Granted, I am playing the devil's advocate a little because when you do have
> the right balance, then Thoughts Betrayed is basically a ticket to torpor, or
> often worse, a precursor to a Walk of Flame and a burnt vampire. The rewards
> are far greater than the 'penalty' of waiting for the right 5 cards to fill
> your hand.

Your statement here is valid.

> I think maybe TB could be fairer if it didn't let your opponent
> strike (like immortal grapple) but still allowed a press to end or
> fortitude. Or maybe something like, your opponent cannot use cards to
> end combat, but could still strike (though that eliminates the
> defensive use of TB).

See my post on a myriad of alternate TB card-texts.
Comments are welcome.

The Assamites' rush options are no more amazing than any Camarilla options:

ground here.)

Messages.Author: Dan Hollis
Messages.Body:
Thomas Doehne wrote:
>
> What about Fast Reaction? Intercept combat, an in-clan skill. gives
> a free round of strikes, with a press at superior. What more
> do you want? Tremere are the best combat clan with a *common*
> in-clan card that gives them a free round of strikes.

I didn't think of it - probably because Tremere strikes are, for
the most part, second round. Fast Reaction is best used, IMO, to
live through a first round against other combat decks. It also gives
you an opportunity to do slight damage (2 or 3) to a vampire who would
otherwise S:CE.
You could give Gangrel out of clan disciplines to play those 'free
round
of strikes' cards, so they could play their aggravated hand strikes.
That
may be a pain in the neck, but the Tremere couldn't get a free second
round
strike at all without Thoughts Betrayed.

But ...

> Blood to Water/Blood Fury should do enough damage to put most vampires
> to bed in one round. Maybe you're not able to burn vampires with the
> second round aggro damage, but you can still use Pulled Fangs on
> the first round. I'd say Tremere have less trouble with S:CE than
> Gangrel. After all, some of them have Celerity (Psyche), too.
>

My lack of Ancient Hearts cards gets me here. I looked up Blood
to Water to refresh my memory, and I agree with you. It's a much
better card for game design than Thoughts Betrayed. Fast reaction,
a 1st round Theft or Blood Fury, and blood to water is a much better
approach for trumping a strike:combat ends. It does hammer a vampire
without the second round strike, and there's the bonus of, with a
Walk of Flame, having a very good chance of an additional 2R aggro'ed
damage if your opponent doesn't have a S:CE anyway. It's such a stylish
workaround, too. :-) No really, both S:CE and TB are so blunt and
boring; they take the card interplay out of the game.

What always bugged me about S:CE is that it is 1 card that it
defeats a whole strategy, and very un-Jyhad like. I wouldn't want
to see a reaction that caused a vote to automatically fail, and
Archon Investigation goes too far against bleed decks.
Thoughts betrayed, as a trump card that trumps only S:CE I
am still moderately okay with, though (the 'my card hoses
your card' attitude is a mtg pitfall which this would come awfully
close to). If it did just burn a S:CE, then you'd have hand
jams to worry about if your opponent doesn't play with S:CE, and
too many will displace more useful combat cards. So, my suggestion,
is to make tb more like Drawing Out the Beast, but with the
addition of not allowing the opposing minion to play a S:CE.
Ultimately, my biggest problem with Thoughts Betrayed is that it
also trumps other combat and fortitude damage prevention.

dh

Messages.Author: Thetmes
Messages.Body:
In response to the Corrupter's reply dated September 9, 1996

>> 2.) Return to innocence

> I don't particularly see this as a trump card. What is your reasoning?

I see this to be a trump card because of the power of the card, and
because in certain situations the only way to stop it is with another
trump (Archon invest). The only defenses against RTI are bounce (until
the end when you can't), AI, or block. This forces every deck to include
bounce (which is rapidly happening in our group), lots of intercept, or
lots of AI to be safe. When I run a deck with RTI in it I begin to
salivate when I see my prey put out Nosferatsu, Settites, Gangrel,
Assimites, Brujah, or anything else without much bounce or intercept. I
have frequently minion tapped an I.C. or other large vamp and bled for
10 to 14 points at stealth to abruptly (and prematurely) end someone's
game. If you plan it right you can have another vamp ready to come out,
or a possession ready so the RTI burning doesn't matter that much. I
did this once at the L.A. tournament (to oust a excellent Settite deck
that was ready to run away with the game) and was also a victim of it.
It is a game ender.

>> 5.) Possibly pulled fangs and tomb of Ramses.

> Both of these I also don't see a trumps (though Pulled Fangs has

> become too powerful with the new aggro ruling). Again, could you
> explain your reasoning?

With the new aggro rule and the ruling on Rotschreck that won't let you
play it against pulled fangs it has become the torpor trump. People
around here have developed infinite ways to use it. "I do 2 hand
damage and pull your fangs", "I prevent my damage and pull your
fangs", or "You dodged, I'll do a additional strike and pull your fangs",
etc. It is one thing to bashed for 9 points by a Brujah and have it
played to burn you, but all the ticky tack ways I am seeing it used here
really make seem like a trump that can only be stopped by SC:E,
obedience, or elysium. One thing for sure even if it is not a trump it is
sure getting aggravating (excuse the word usage).

Tomb of Ramses might not meet the definition of trump your looking
for, but it has a extreme effect on the game. More than a couple times I
have gotten one of these suckers out on the first turn and brought out
two I.C.s or other large vamps in three turns. Every time I get one at
the beginning of the game everyone checks for sudden reversals, and
there is a large mutual groan (sometimes accented with cursing) if
nobody has one. My winning percentage since I got 4 tombs is over
50%. To me it seems like to big a advantage if you use large vamps.

> Thanks.

Your welcome.

> lose my malk bleeder he\she only had one blood anyway who cares, I get
> another or use the other 3 that I have because I have more vampires
> because of the minion taps.

S&B is not a problem. It may be difficult to play against, but a
combat deck should be able to pound vampires with 1 blood. A vote deck
may have a bit more trouble, but could always change seating order, Ventrue
and Toreador can bounce the bleed, or the deck could call damaging votes.
And first, the vampire that you're about to minion tap is going to have to
live through a turn without losing the blood you plan to get back. Which
most likely won't happen if you're next to a rush combat deck.
How much avoid combat does the deck have? With enough minion taps to
consistantly grab pool before you lose it to combat, or with enough taps to
handle a sudden reversal, then you're going to have to take something out of
the deck. Let me guess that it's not going to be stealth or bleed, since
that's the focus of the deck and I'll assume you've tuned it so you already
have the right ratio. Maybe some bleed bounce, or maybe some anti-combat?
Oh, and how are you going to play a conditioning, legal manipulations,
or govern the unaligned with a stripped minion?
I don't see you can get this to work well; how you can really not care about
losing a vampire, most likely somewhat large to have the stealth & bleed skills
you need. You've added a whole new aspect to the deck (cardwise, you're going
to be less efficient), and made yourself more susceptible to combat, especially
rush combat.

Dh

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On 11 Sep 1996, Thetmes wrote:

> In response to the Corrupter's reply dated September 9, 1996

> >> 2.) Return to innocence

> > I don't particularly see this as a trump card. What is your reasoning?

> I see this to be a trump card because of the power of the card,

Which I'm not to concerned with. The card is dead weight until mid/late
game. A dead card in hand is a _huge_ detriment in Jyhad.

> and
> because in certain situations the only way to stop it is with another
> trump (Archon invest).

This I can see.

> The only defenses against RTI are bounce (until
> the end when you can't), AI, or block.

Another "defense" is placing a predator in such a weak position (via
Rush, Back-bleeding/voting, etc.) that losing that vampire is not worth
the cost. One thing to note, this only really works if people play to
_win_ the game, not just oust _a_ prey. (This game really begins to
break down if people aren't trying to win.)

>This forces every deck to include
> bounce (which is rapidly happening in our group), lots of intercept, or
> lots of AI to be safe. When I run a deck with RTI in it I begin to
> salivate when I see my prey put out Nosferatsu, Settites, Gangrel,
> Assimites, Brujah, or anything else without much bounce or intercept. I
> have frequently minion tapped an I.C. or other large vamp and bled for
> 10 to 14 points at stealth to abruptly (and prematurely) end someone's
> game. If you plan it right you can have another vamp ready to come out,
> or a possession ready so the RTI burning doesn't matter that much. I
> did this once at the L.A. tournament (to oust a excellent Settite deck
> that was ready to run away with the game) and was also a victim of it.
> It is a game ender.

This is a valid point. I don't like the idea of seeing a game brought to
an abrupt halt like RTI could do.

My total position on RTI is thus:
I don't think the card is too inexpensive, in fact (do to its
hand-jamming), I think it is priced correctly.
However, I don't think the card has a place in the game. (I do think it
is a trump, or at least a semi-trump.) To make an analogy to another
card, if Thoughts Betrayed cost 3 blood, I would feel that the cost was
appropriate, but I still wouldn't feel comfortable with a card like it in
the playset (It's more a Magic card than a Jyhad card).

> >> 5.) Possibly pulled fangs and tomb of Ramses.

> > Both of these I also don't see a trumps (though Pulled Fangs has
> > become too powerful with the new aggro ruling). Again, could you
> > explain your reasoning?

[multiple examples of ease of Pulling Fangs]

I'm not convinced Pulled Fangs is a trump, though with the new V:tES
agg-damage, I think it is too powerful. IMHO, errata to make the damage
zero would be appropriate (but if one damage is not "prevented" the
vampire goes to torpor).

> Tomb of Ramses might not meet the definition of trump your looking
> for, but it has a extreme effect on the game. More than a couple times I
> have gotten one of these suckers out on the first turn and brought out
> two I.C.s or other large vamps in three turns. Every time I get one at
> the beginning of the game everyone checks for sudden reversals, and
> there is a large mutual groan (sometimes accented with cursing) if
> nobody has one. My winning percentage since I got 4 tombs is over
> 50%. To me it seems like to big a advantage if you use large vamps.

I wouldn't consider this a trump either, but it is definately undercosted.

In case people are wondering, I consider a "trump" to be a card which
forces people to have certain specific defenses or die, or a card that
disallows certain _entire_ strategies. Thoughts
Betrayed is such a card, as it requires permanent combat ability from the
opponent. Archon Investigation is such a card, as it not only stops big
bleeds, but destroys the Methuselah even attempting to do one. This
might cause someone to feel that Elder Kindred Network is such a card,
but Elder Kindred Network is still something relatively preventable.

(The above is not too clear, but then, I've only had 3 hours sleep (and
upwards of a quart of coffee... :)



[smacks his forehead] Well, that's the single most important reason, and
I'm surprised that I was so heavily in rant-mode that I didn't get that
across... sorry...

> AI is still out of line with the Jyhad cardset; it's still a "may
> as well get a Coke" card when you're hit with it.

Then again, you are kind of asking for it. In a combat deck, for
example, you have to consider all of the possible things your opponent
can do; press, maneuver, have guns, have additional strikes, have Thau,
have S:CE, etc. But in S&B, the only thing you would have to worry
about is not getting blocked. And unless your prey is a full-fledged
auspex intercept deck, you probably won't have a problem. So, now, with
AI, you have something to worry about. Just like someone in combat with
the Gangrel has to worry about getting poked in the eye, you have to
worry about AI. You don't _have_ to bleed for more than 3. That's your
choice.

Question: How is this card being played in decks? Do people have
multiple copies?
Do big bleeders get burned constantly? It hasn't been much of a problem
around here...

> happens in combat, at superior he's tapped and you're untapped) so I
> have
> it filed mentally with S:CE. I agree that it is also a problem, and
> that
> many S:CE fixes will not help with Obedience.

Yes, the problem is that even the few things that help against S:CE
don't help against Obedience.

This leads me to a new card idea:

Assassinate
Action
Potence
Inf: (D) Attack a minion of your predator or prey at +1 stealth.
Sup: As above, and for the remainer of this action, the controller of
that minion may not play reaction cards.

This stops obedience, but isn't much more powerful than Bum's Rush.

James

IMO, James, Assassinate is a more powerful card than Bum's Rush
at superior. Bum's Rush could be blocked more easily, and
Auspex-Animalism has no chance of intercepting the Assassinate action.
No reaction cards may be played. You might want to reword it so that

If someone made a deck which is specifically able to deal with the weaknesses
of almost all of the other decks in the enviroment, then they'll probably win.
This is true of almost any type of deck. Solution? Make the enviroment less
homogenous, or just beat the S&B deck at its own game. Bruise and bleed; tap and
bleed, tap and fight. Hey, that one's not a bad idea, if you're really worried

Well, effectively, you are. The bleed would have been successful(ie. you
either couldn't block or chose not to just so you could burn the vampire),
so effectively you are a) gaining pool, or at least not losing as much as
you would have, b) Burning a vampire of your predator's for no additional
other than the (effective) gain of pool, c) negating the success of the bleed,
so that your predator does not gain the edge. From my perspective, If I've
spent 13 pool and an action transferring out Leandro, Playing a Legendary
Vampire one him, and Giving him a Pulse of the Canaille, and someone can play one
card, cancel my bleed, and burn a vampire who I've put a huge amount of pool and
resources into for 3 pool, I would definitely feel that the card that they played
was unfair. Can you see that?

>using your argument on Obedience, no deck is going to have more than 2
>of these things, and many decks won't have any. I'm taking mine out,
>'cause I just got a hold of Protracted Racehorses.

Protected Resources is also an overpowered card, from my perspective
(I will admit that I am a S&B supporter, but...), because it allows your predator
no options as to getting rid of it. It can really cripple a S&B deck, or any other
type of bleed deck which relies on single vampires getting through. Inner
circlers, Vamps with Legendary vampire played on them, and whatever else, only
bleed for 2, at most. Not to mention that their hand will be jamming with bleed
cards which will most likely cost blood. Ick. And it costs no pool, right?

I can just see a disgusting blood machine deck with protected resources out, bleed
bounce and countering, and ways to gain up to four pool a turn. Nasty; and if
they're doing vote damage and/or anarch revolts, it's never going away.

>I'll be frank. I'm just finding it hard for _my_ deck to deal with
>S&B. The intercept angle works really well most of the time. When I

the best potential for permanent intercept(raven spy, sport's bike, KRCG/London
Evening star), but also the best untap ability as well. Unless they've been
pulling superior Elder Impersonations and Seductions on every bleed, it
would seem that you'd be able to get them at least 1/2 the time, and claw them

Gangrel rush doesn't compare to Brujah? Geeze. I was under the impression
that Brujah was slightly inferior. They can't get stealth as easily, picking on
their chosen target; aggravated damage is a lot harder to come by, etc.
And Gangrel, if they can get extra strikes through a vial of Garou blood or Shadow
of the wolf, can make their last strike aggravated and burn people. Or just send
them to torpor. Maybe it's just me, but I've been a lot more frightened by gangrel
decks than by Brujah recently... Maybe it's just the flexibility that the gangrel
seem to have.

But, unless I know more, I can't really make any suggestions or judgements.

Alec Chang

Messages.Author: theCorrupter
Messages.Body:
On 23 Sep 1996, Sorrow wrote:

[The Corrupter wrote:]

> >AI is out of line for three reasons:
> > 1) Inappropriate cost (effectively -X pool to destroy a bleed of 3+X)
> > 2) Unprecedented effect (compare to Golconda)
> > 3) Destruction of an entire strategy with a single card (Magic effect)

> Can you sudden reverse an AI? I don't see any reason why you shouldn't
> be able to...

No, you can't sudden reversal an AI. Sudden Reversal is an out-of-turn
master, and thus, cannot be used on your own turn (according to the
definition of OOT-Master). Only OOT-Masters (like Absolution of th
Diabolist) that _explicitly_ say that they can be used on your on turn,
may be. Otherwise, you would need to convince another player to do it for
you.

Archon Investigation OOT Master 3 Pool

Have you considered the possibility that there's so much combat in your
group that combat decks are in general having a hard time? If everybody

Return to Innocence is a very powerful card, and its'
existence can only be justified by the existence of Archon
Investigation. Spiridonas' special ability can only be justified
by the presence of AI, too.

It burns the vampire bleeding you for 3 pool, preventing a
bleed of more than three. Calculated risks do not involve
losing a fairly large vampire for an incurred penalty of one
card and 3 pool. Calculated risks involve taking a bleed for
another player with a Major Boon.

preponderance of massive bleed modifiers and abilities, and
sets a precedence for even nastier cards which hose over bleed.

> Return to Innocence is a very powerful card, and its'

RtI is the first card in the VtES set that my group's seriously
considering banning. There are so many ways to get vampires back, its
cost isn't relevant, especially in a deck like my Giovanni 'Inconnu'
deck, where Regina got Returned and Possessed back into play to be
Golconda'd next turn. Instead of stealth, I used Clan Impersonation
combined with Clan Loyalty -- a clan with Fortitude or Protean could
easily make use of Day Op or Horrific Countenance.

Which leads to a truly hideous crock deck that isn't covered by the
Golden Tenets -- I'll take the man's $50, but I'll still feel bad about
it.

12 Etrius

10 Return to Innocence
10 Magic of the Smith
10 Soul Gem of Etrius
10 Protean (or Fortitude, if Etrius has no or inferior Fortitude)
10 Horrific Countenance (or Day Op as appropriate)
10 Information Highway
10 Tomb of Rameses III

Etrius is out by turn 2, 3 max. Lay a Skill card on him and Return
to Innocence for 1 +12 +2 = 15 points of unblockable bleed, thanks be
to Day Op or Horrific Countenance. Well, Magic a Soul Gem onto him
first. Then, when he goes pop, you get a fresh Etrius at no extra charge!
And this fresh one already has the Soul Gem. Lay a skill card on him,
Return to Innocence. Repeat as necessary.

Garnish with beak.

What defends against this? Bounce will do it. Intercepting the Magics
will slow it down a little, but it's got to be a moby intercept deck that can
muster +3 intercept regularly by turn 3. And, of course, the antibleed crocks
like AI and Protected Resources.

This kind of thing, possible only with RtI (would you seriously contemplate
a deck like the above with Governs instead of Returns?), essentially
forces everyone to play bounce/intercept. Combat is essentially
helpless against this, as is vote. It's Dominate and Auspex, all the way --
hey, who has those two disciplines again?

I'm open to suggestions to fix RtI. Two proposed fixes:

4 blood action.
+X bleed, where X = Vampire's Capacity/2 (Round Down). Usable only by
a vampire with a capacity above 7. No bleed enhancing modifiers may be
played. Burn vampire if successful.

Maximum bleed with the above is 8 with an IC (1 +5 +2), so I might be
amenable to not burning the vampire, but just knocking into torpor with
a 'cannot rescue self' flag.

4 blood action.
When the action is declared, vampire may burn X+2 blood for +X bleed. No
bleed enhancing modifiers may be played. Burn vampire if successful.
Usable only by a vampire with a capacity above 7.

This one's a Spiridonas Reconstruction Kit; max bleed here is also 8
(11-4=7, to burn for +5 bleed, +2 inherent = 8), so a similar caveat applies.

gomi

Messages.Author: theCorrupter
Messages.Body:
> return to innocence has disturbing implications for the game as a whole

Thank you, Gomi No Sensei.
Well, it has finally been done.

Someone has built a broken deck using the Golden Tenets (no repeat action
/ no vote push).

For those of you who are unaware of the ongoing saga, for some time I have
claimed that it could not be done. I even went so far as to recently add
a cash value to the first person who could actually do it.

Now, thanks to Ancient Hearts, and mostly the precedent set by Archon
Investigation, it has been done.

The card that makes it possible is Return to Innocence. By itself, Return
to Innocence is an expensive, clunky card. Put into just any old deck,
and it really isn't too much of a threat: the card is expensive, not
useful in early game, and could easily backfire on the user. However, in
a deck built to exploit it, easily a broken card.

As someone else pointed out, this card is (yet another) trump card.
Basicly, it forces people to play deflection or (sometimes) high
intercept. The risk is too great, now, not to. The card is held in line
by another (broken) card, Archon Investigation.

So it looks like, now, Jyhad has finally degenerated to a game of trumps,
albeit just barely.

Here is the deck, along with my feelings of how it could be improved on
the side [in Brackets]

On 27 Sep 1996, Gomi no Sensei wrote:
> Which leads to a truly hideous crock deck that isn't covered by the
> Golden Tenets -- I'll take the man's $50, but I'll still feel bad about
> it.

> 12 Etrius [I would change this to 14 Etrius.
This gives you the ability to use all
of the Return to Innocence without
exhausting your crypt.]

> 10 Return to Innocence
> 10 Magic of the Smith
> 10 Soul Gem of Etrius
> 10 Protean (or Fortitude, if Etrius has no or inferior Fortitude)
> 10 Horrific Countenance (or Day Op as appropriate)

> 10 Information Highway [I would reduce this to at most 4. The
speed of getting out a quick Etrius is
Outweighed by the hand jam]
> 10 Tomb of Rameses III [I would take these out altogether]
[Add in up to 3 The Barrens (to cycle)]
[My version: 55 Cards]

The only real defenses against the deck are _extremely_ fast high
intercept and deflection. Other tertiary defenses are contesting the
vampire or the Soul Gem.

Solutions to the problem:

[Re: Return to Innocence]

> RtI is the first card in the VtES set that my group's seriously
> considering banning.

Banning works, but is not something I relish.

> I'm open to suggestions to fix RtI. Two proposed fixes:

> 4 blood action.
> +X bleed, where X = Vampire's Capacity/2 (Round Down). Usable only by
> a vampire with a capacity above 7. No bleed enhancing modifiers may be
> played. Burn vampire if successful.

> 4 blood action.
> When the action is declared, vampire may burn X+2 blood for +X bleed. No
> bleed enhancing modifiers may be played. Burn vampire if successful.
> Usable only by a vampire with a capacity above 7.

I don't particularly care for either of these.

How about:

The Return to Innocence (Fixed???) - 4 blood - Action
(D) Bleed your prey at +X, where X is the capacity of the vampire.
Burn this vampire if the bleed is successful. Action Modifiers may not be
used on this action.

---

> return to innocence has disturbing implications for the game as a whole

That it does. That it does.

Well, Gomi No Sensei is the proud recipient of $50. E-mail me for info,
GNS.

I am convinced that this case is an aberration. If anyone else can come
up with a degenerate deck using No Limit / Golden Tenet House Rules, I
still challenge you. Of course, given Ian and Leatherface, the Sabbat
might make it really easy.

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <Pine.GUL.3.95.960927...@yar.cs.wisc.edu>,

theCorrupter <adr...@yar.cs.wisc.edu> wrote:
>> return to innocence has disturbing implications for the game as a whole
>
>Thank you, Gomi No Sensei.
>Well, it has finally been done.

although I must admit I take little pleasure in it.

>[Re: Return to Innocence]
>> RtI is the first card in the VtES set that my group's seriously
>> considering banning.
>
>Banning works, but is not something I relish.

Well, we'd certainly prefer a good fix -- we just couldn't come up with
one off the bat last night.

>How about:
>
>The Return to Innocence (Fixed???) - 4 blood - Action
>(D) Bleed your prey at +X, where X is the capacity of the vampire.
>Burn this vampire if the bleed is successful. Action Modifiers may not be
>used on this action.

I like it. It's concise and elegant. How about 'This action may not be
modified' instead, to rule out permanent stealth such as Opium Den or,
more seriously, Forest of Shadows?

you can still get through an unblockable return with Blood Bonds, but if
you invest the time and energy in blood bonding all your prey's
minions, more power to ya, i think. i think that, by changing the final
clause to 'this action may not be modified', enough bases are covered to
get it in line.

A more fundamental issue of design is how far cost/benefit goes. Return
is predicated on a theoretically hideous cost -- axing a vampire.
Unfortunately, non-pool costs are harder to balance -- Soul Gems or
Possession make a mockery of Return's cost. Depravity is another
example -- a deck without allies or retainers gets free bonuses. Another
poorly thought out cost is Blythe Candeleria -- what was the last
Tremere deck you saw that relied on its hand damage?

There are, i think, some levels of power that no cost justifies; either
a deck is built solely to afford that cost, and gains immense power
thereby, or the cost is prohibitive to regular decks. You'll notice
no retainer, ally, or equipment (yet) costs more than 5 pool, and no
master card more than 3 (barring Misdirection, which is a special case).
Exceeding these costs would be a Bad Thing in my estimation; an ally so
good as to be worth 7 pool would be too good. A location so useful as
to be worth 5 pool would be way too good.

My point, i guess, is this: there are ways to defeat any cost; the best
way to avoid the problems that raises is to make it, in general, not
worth the bother, and so the benefit conferred by any single card
must be kept below a certain threshold that Return to Innocence
crosses, batons twirling.

At high power levels, additonally, small errors in cost/power are much
more critical, resulting either in wallpaper or must-haves. It might
be argued that Skin of Steel should be worth less than, say, Blood Fury,
but at that relatively small scale of benefits it's just easier to
pay the 1 blood and move along with one's life.

>Well, Gomi No Sensei is the proud recipient of $50. E-mail me for info,
>GNS.

whoopie. making money never bummed me out before.

>I am convinced that this case is an aberration. If anyone else can come
>up with a degenerate deck using No Limit / Golden Tenet House Rules, I
>still challenge you. Of course, given Ian and Leatherface, the Sabbat
>might make it really easy.

Let's wait n see. Sigh.

i agree with you on the aberration bit, and can only hope that this sort
of thing fails to continue.

gomi

Messages.Author: Alec Chang
Messages.Body:
In article <52hv92$l...@shellx.best.com>, go...@best.com says...
(snipped commentary specific to the 'fixing' of Return to Innocence.)

>A more fundamental issue of design is how far cost/benefit goes. Return
>is predicated on a theoretically hideous cost -- axing a vampire.
>Unfortunately, non-pool costs are harder to balance -- Soul Gems or
>Possession make a mockery of Return's cost.

I've noticed that over time, the most degenerate effects come, usually not
from single cards without clearly defined and balanced abilities, but the
use of multiple cards of these types, which combine to create a combination
which is nauseatingly unbalanced. Also, this kind of problem could have
been thought of by the playtesters, and fairly easily if they were
seriously TRYING to break each expansion card. Both of the cards that
Return is broken with are in previous sets, and should have been taken into
consideration. This may say something about Jyhad/V:tES and playtesting
priority at WotC.

>Depravity is another example -- a deck without allies or retainers gets
>free bonuses. Another poorly thought out cost is Blythe Candeleria --
>what was the last Tremere deck you saw that relied on its hand damage?

Generic cards, especially in Jyhad, should have major restrictions on their
play and use, like Legendary Vampire has. Depravity, although not
unbalancing on it's own, can be compared to a bastard sword, and found to
be almost infinitely better, even with it's being unique.

Blythe, however, is a different matter, in that NOTHING that I can see
justifies the idea that -1 hand damage vs. malkavians(not usually a
dangerous combat clan by any stretch) is worth even 1 extra point in
disciplines, much less the two that were printed(and I agree with Nathan
here; it does seem that Blythe was intentionally made that way and when
players objected, then she was errataed). Tremere bias, again.

This becomes even more apparent when one realizes that there were a number
of five and six capacity vampires in the same expansion who were vastly
underpowered from almost any perspective.(Andrei Puxon, Vittorio Giovanni,
Sigrid Bekker...).

>There are, i think, some levels of power that no cost justifies; either
>a deck is built solely to afford that cost, and gains immense power
>thereby, or the cost is prohibitive to regular decks. You'll notice
>no retainer, ally, or equipment (yet) costs more than 5 pool, and no
>master card more than 3 (barring Misdirection, which is a special case).
>Exceeding these costs would be a Bad Thing in my estimation; an ally so
>good as to be worth 7 pool would be too good. A location so useful as
>to be worth 5 pool would be way too good.

Right on. But levels of power are usually relative, especially in the
more specialized rare cards. Cards which may seem useless become over-
powered when broken. The primary reason why this seems to occur is A)
not enough playtesting with abuse taken into account, and B)an insufficient
grasp on what constitutes a balance between cost and effect, especially in
circumstances where the cost can be circumvented. Netrunner and Magic have
this same kind of problem; when drawbacks of certain cards(Organ Donor,
Ernham Djinn) can be easily gotten around by certain strategies or specific
other cards, they begin to dominate and break the game.

>My point, i guess, is this: there are ways to defeat any cost; the best
>way to avoid the problems that raises is to make it, in general, not
>worth the bother, and so the benefit conferred by any single card
>must be kept below a certain threshold that Return to Innocence
>crosses, batons twirling.

Return doesn't do it as blatantly as, say, Spiridonas. Return is broken in
the deck that you postulated, which took people a while to work
out. Spiridonas screams for abuse right out of a booster. When in a deck
designed to exploit him, he can bleed for a huge amount one turn,
Hospitality himself(in the same turn, even, with a Rutor's hand in play),
and keep up pressure on one's prey. With Info Highways and Tombs of
Rameses, he can come out early enough so that a few seductions could keep
him from being blocked at all. Not totally broken, but disgusting and
needing no real skill or intelligence to pull off nonetheless.

>At high power levels, additonally, small errors in cost/power are much
>more critical, resulting either in wallpaper or must-haves. It might
>be argued that Skin of Steel should be worth less than, say, Blood Fury,
>but at that relatively small scale of benefits it's just easier to
>pay the 1 blood and move along with one's life.

It can be argued, but I find that the commons are often much better costed
and balanced than the rares. Commons are usually made with some system in
mind, and the uncommons tend to have the same system, just made more
specialized and powerful, as well as expensive. Rares are often when
designers seem to start "Coloring outside the lines" and making monumental
design errors which only show up when people start breaking cards. Perhaps
the amount of playtesting needed would be excessive; but as of now, it
seems that it's insufficient, especially on V:tES.

>>Well, Gomi No Sensei is the proud recipient of $50. E-mail me for info,
>>GNS.
>
>whoopie. making money never bummed me out before.
>
>>I am convinced that this case is an aberration. If anyone else can come
>>up with a degenerate deck using No Limit / Golden Tenet House Rules, I
>>still challenge you. Of course, given Ian and Leatherface, the Sabbat
>>might make it really easy.
>
>Let's wait n see. Sigh.
>
>i agree with you on the aberration bit, and can only hope that this sort
>of thing fails to continue.
>

Well, Nathan and I haven't completely broken the game with the overpowered
Tremere stuff yet, but we haven't seen everything from Sabbat yet. I hope
we don't succeed; but we may have to voluntarily not use the cards which
are broken, and PROVE to our friends that there's something wrong so that
they go along too. Sigh. We still play 4-CL, so this may take us some
doing...

Alec Chang

Even with the fixes suggested so far, i`m not sure whether those will be much
of a help.

There are quite a few ways to get control of other vampires (Malkavian
Dementia, Temptation, Form of Corruption... ). While this is bad news for the
player in question already, RtI now offers an additional way to burn this
vampire.

especially if there`s an interest to keep the original owner in the game.

severly shifts the balance of the game. As long as you add some stealth it
doesn`t matter whether you get bounced or suffer from an AI. The vampire will

later in this post) If Nathan's hypothesis is correct(and I have no
reason to believe that it isn't, given that I cannnot see anyone
seeing Spiridonas and RTI as reasonable, balanced cards, except
through a Tremere bias and the idea that "AI balances them out")
then the cards which we see as unbalancing/overpowered/trumps create
more cards which we consider to be escalating negative trends.

>(Or perhaps, any other strategy.)

Just as a reminder to people out there who think "Well, it's only
big bleed that's getting hosed, and it deserves it anyway"... If
this kind of thing goes on, every strategy will have to deal with
trump cards.

>-Nathan Harada

>up with a degenerate deck using No Limit / Golden Tenet House Rules, I
>still challenge you. Of course, given Ian and Leatherface, the Sabbat

From what I've seen, the biggest targets look like Tremere Bruise/
Bleed with obfuscate, first round ags, and thoughts betrayed.

I think Nathan posted a variation on this earlier; and we don't know
if there are any more cards in Sabbat which would make that deck more
degenerate than it is now(everytime that It's played, it's swept the table).

But my point isn't that certain cards are broken or overpowered; but more
that WotC's lack of concern about these cards, and also the lack of concern
about these cards by players, which leads to more ignoring of problems by
WotC, leads to the creation of more degenerate cards which, as they pile
up, will profoundly warp, if not totally wreck the balance of this game we
play.

So, please guys, listen. Don't just stick your heels in about cards; listen
to the arguments, read the posts, and TRY to see how the cards can be broken.
The issue is NOT if the card can be played in a reasonable manner, but if
the card can be played in a broken or overpowered manner. We'll probably
have to define what broken is, as each of us will have their own definition.
But if we want to stop what the majority of us percieve as a downward slide
in the balance of the cards being created by WotC, we've got to speak up
about our concerns, Talk to Shawn in a reasonable and calm manner, so he'll
actually pay attention to us, and get our arguments ironed out. Point.
By point. By point.

I hate to be melodramatic, but the issue here is that the game has been
broken, directly as a result of RTI, and indirectly as a result of AI.
I shudder to think what might occur if we do not say or do something
about this trend NOW. And some of us are still saying "have faith in
WotC" and denying that there's a problem...

Anyway, no offense to anyone, but do we have to provide more evidence
that this trend on WotC's part is really messing up the game? Please,
back us up so that this game that we love doesn't go down the tubes.

Alec Chang,

a Very Concerned Gamer resorting to rhetoric to get his point across.

> _other_ minion. IMHO, well-designed S&B decks are fast enough that the
> loss of a vampire is relatively easily dealt with.

With all due respect to James, I think people are focusing way too
much on AI vs. S&B, and not enough on AI vs other bleed decks.
Tap-and-bleed and bruise-and-bleed rarely can get more than one or
two bleeds each turn. Against many decks, one or two bleeds a turn is
irrelevant, unless both those bleeds are big- 3 or more points. However,
AI hoses those bleeds, and the bleeder.
Think about it. Your predator has Masika w/ flak jacket and a
submachinegun and Aire of Elation in hand. You have a Ren. Garou, two
untapped minions, and 5 pool. Your prey has 2 pool and is tapped out, no
wakes. Oh, and you have AI. When Masika comes a-bleeding, do you block,
and probably lose a minion, or take the bleed and destroy Masika with AI?
(A similar situation happened to me last week, only I had the Toreador
deck. Fortunately, my prey did _not_ have AI. If he had, I would have
lost).
Given the choice between blocking, or just spending three pool to
destroy a vampire, which would anyone choose? Fight Donal and lose a
minion, or destroy Donal at minimal cost?
AI might be balanced against S&B, I'm not sure. Against all other
bleed forms, its not. Can we move the argument in that direction?

-Mark Langsdorf
